Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Situation2: They notice minor inconsistencies in a building plan that are unlikely to cause immediate issues.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was reviewing the final building plans for tomorrow’s inspection. It was late, and the office was empty except for the hum of the fluorescent lights. I glanced at the screen—my best friend, Sam. I answered, and his panicked voice spilled out: his car had broken down on the highway, miles from anywhere, and he needed me to pick him up right away. I promised I’d figure something out, but as I hung up, my eyes drifted back to the plans on my desk. There were minor inconsistencies in the fire escape routes—nothing catastrophic, but enough to nag at my conscience. As the architect, I was expected to ensure every detail was safe and compliant, no matter how small. If I left now, I’d miss my only chance to fix the plans before the morning review. But Sam was counting on me, scared and stranded. My chest tightened as I weighed the responsibility to my friend against my duty as an architect, feeling the pressure of both roles pulling me in opposite directions.
